summaries.example: Three friends are choosing a shared gift. Two want a book and dinner; one wants neither. A majority choice gives both the book and dinner. An arbitration-style choice tries to spread the disappointment more evenly, perhaps choosing only one of the two gifts. The example shows that different rules can treat disagreement differently.
summaries.summary: When people, computers, or databases have different information, they may need one shared answer. The information can conflict, especially when the questions are logically connected. Judgment aggregation studies how to turn individual judgments into a group judgment. Belief merging studies how to fuse several belief bases—sets of statements—into one consistent base. A simple majority can fail: the group may accept statements that cannot all be true together. Merging methods avoid this by considering possible complete situations and selecting those that best fit the sources while obeying any required conditions. Different methods measure “best fit” differently. A majority method tries to reduce the total disagreement, while an arbitration method tries to prevent one person from being much more unhappy than the others. These ideas connect philosophy, logic, social choice, and computer science.
key_ideas: Groups often need to combine opinions about questions that are connected by rules.
A majority vote on each question can sometimes create a group answer that breaks a logical rule.
Belief merging is designed to combine possibly conflicting information into a consistent result.
Some methods favor what most sources say; others try to share disagreement fairly.
A method can avoid inconsistency by considering the whole set of questions instead of treating every question separately.
summaries.why_it_matters: Shared decisions appear in courts, councils, schools, online ratings, computer systems, and databases. A method for combining information should not just count answers; it should also avoid contradictions and respect important rules. Studying these methods helps us see why group decisions can be difficult and why there is no single perfect rule for every situation.

important_terms.definition: A way for a group to combine people’s answers about several connected questions.
Combining information from several sources into one consistent set of beliefs or statements.
A rule or fact that the final answer must obey, such as a budget limit.
A measure of how different two possible answers are. A smaller distance means closer.
A surprising result in which each person’s answers make sense, but the group’s combined answers do not fit together.

questions_to_think_about: Should a group always use majority rule?
When two sources disagree, what would make one source more trustworthy?
Is it fairer to choose what most people want, or to spread disappointment evenly?
Why might a rule about a budget change the group’s answer?

summaries.example: Consider a three-member court deciding whether a defendant is liable. Let p mean that a contract forbade an action, q mean that the defendant performed it, and r mean that the defendant is liable. The legal rule says r holds exactly when both p and q hold. Each judge gives a logically consistent set of answers. Yet proposition-wise majority gives p, q, and not-r: a majority supports both conditions but rejects the conclusion. A distance-based merging rule instead compares possible interpretations that obey the legal rule and chooses those closest to the judges’ positions. It may produce several tied outcomes, so a tie-breaking rule could be needed.
summaries.summary: Judgment aggregation and belief merging address related but distinct problems. Judgment aggregation starts with a specified agenda of logically connected propositions and asks how to produce a collective judgment set. Belief merging starts with several belief bases, represented in propositional logic, and seeks a consistent base, often under integrity constraints. The distinction matters because majority judgments can be individually consistent yet collectively inconsistent. In the court example, majorities on premises and conclusion conflict with the rule connecting them. Impossibility theorems show that, on rich agendas, no non-dictatorial rule can simultaneously guarantee broad input, logically rational outputs, proposition-by-proposition independence, and unanimity preservation. Belief-merging operators offer another route: they compare possible interpretations, discard those violating constraints, and select the closest remaining ones. A sum-based distance favors collective popularity; other operators attend to the largest individual loss or to a more even distribution. These approaches can preserve consistency, but they may be irresolute, computationally difficult, sensitive to the chosen distance, or open to strategic manipulation. They also differ in their inputs, treatment of abstention, and assumptions about reliability.
key_ideas: The doctrinal or discursive dilemma shows that individually rational judgments can yield a collectively irrational result under proposition-wise majority rule.
Judgment aggregation imposes conditions such as universal domain, collective rationality, independence, and unanimity preservation.
Impossibility results show that, for sufficiently rich agendas, these conditions cannot all be met by a non-dictatorial rule.
Belief merging uses integrity constraints and selects a consistent outcome from possibilities that are closest to the information sources.
Minisum aggregates Hamming distances by adding them, while minimax and leximax represent different concerns about the worst-off or the distribution of disagreement.
Merging avoids the standard impossibility result partly because it gives up independence: judgments on one proposition may depend on the wider logical structure.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic reveals a general tension between democratic responsiveness, logical consistency, fairness, and resistance to manipulation. It applies to courts and councils as well as expert panels, databases, sensors, and multi-agent systems. Rather than proving that one method is universally correct, the theory clarifies which values a rule protects and which it sacrifices. That makes formal analysis useful when designing procedures for real collective reasoning.

important_terms.definition: The study of rules for combining individual judgments on propositions into a collective judgment.
The study of combining several independent, possibly conflicting belief bases into a consistent base.
A set of propositions on which individuals are asked to accept or reject items, including their negations.
A group of judgments that is both complete and logically consistent.
A condition that the collective result must satisfy, such as a legal rule or a budget restriction.
A rule requiring each proposition’s group judgment to depend only on individual judgments about that proposition.
A procedure that chooses interpretations minimizing some measure of disagreement with the sources.
An approach minimizing total disagreement; arbitration instead focuses on distributing disagreement more evenly.

questions_to_think_about: Is independence worth keeping if it can permit inconsistent collective judgments?
Should an aggregation rule aim at the most popular answer or at the fairest distribution of disagreement?
What is lost when a method selects several tied outcomes rather than one?
How do integrity constraints change what counts as an acceptable group judgment?
Should information sources be treated equally when their reliability differs?

summaries.example: Imagine a student council choosing projects for a courtyard. Members answer two connected questions: whether to build a garden and whether to build a play area. A rule says that if both are built, the budget must also include extra maintenance money. Each student’s answers obeys this rule. But if the council takes a separate majority vote on each question, the combined result might approve both projects while rejecting the maintenance money. The group answer is then inconsistent. A belief-merging method would compare only plans that obey the budget rule and choose the plans closest to everyone’s views.
summaries.summary: Groups often combine opinions about issues that affect one another. This happens in courts, councils, expert panels, online ratings, and computer systems. Judgment aggregation asks how individual judgments can become a collective judgment. Belief merging asks how several information bases can be fused into one consistent base. The difficulty is that separate majority decisions can clash with the logical rules linking the questions. In a court case, for example, a majority might support both conditions for liability while a majority rejects liability itself. Every judge can be consistent while the group is not. Formal results show that no non-dictatorial aggregation rule can always satisfy several attractive requirements at once, including accepting all reasonable individual inputs, producing a consistent group result, treating each issue independently, and respecting unanimity. Belief merging takes a different path. It uses integrity constraints and compares possible interpretations by distance. A sum-based method favors the option with the least total disagreement. Arbitration methods focus more on fairness between sources. These methods can preserve consistency, but they may produce ties and depend on choices about distance, reliability, and the constraints being used.
key_ideas: Connected questions create special problems for group decisions because separate majorities may not fit together.
The doctrinal paradox is a famous court example of this problem.
Judgment aggregation seeks group judgments that remain rational, but important goals can conflict.
Belief merging treats information sources as belief bases and uses constraints to rule out unacceptable results.
Majority-style merging minimizes total disagreement, while arbitration-style merging tries to make disagreement more evenly shared.
Distance-based procedures may leave several equally good answers, so another rule may be needed to choose one.
summaries.why_it_matters: Collective reasoning is not merely a matter of counting hands. The way a group combines answers can change the result, especially when reasons and conclusions are connected. Belief merging gives philosophers and computer scientists tools for handling conflicting databases, expert reports, sensors, and opinions. Learning about these tools helps us ask a useful question: what should a decision rule value most—popularity, consistency, fairness, or something else?

important_terms.definition: Combining people’s answers about several related statements to form one group answer.
Combining several sets of information, even when they conflict, into one consistent set.
A collection of questions or statements that people must judge as accepted or rejected.
A rule that says which combinations of answers are allowed.
A group answer that covers the questions and does not contradict the rules connecting them.
A condition saying that the group’s answer on one statement should depend only on votes about that statement.
A number or comparison showing how far a possible group answer is from an individual’s information.

questions_to_think_about: Would you rather have the most popular group answer or one that treats each member more equally?
Why might voting on reasons and voting on a final decision lead to different results?
Should a group be allowed to leave a question unanswered?
What kinds of rules should count as integrity constraints in a school decision?
Can a method be logical but still feel unfair?
